intel.title: Q-learning glossary — four terms to start

facTools.title: Workshop kits
facTools.desc: One printable kit per mission: glossary, references, race table, facilitator notes. A team scoresheet consolidates the three missions on one page.

glossary.agent:
AGENT
An agent is the entity making decisions: a person or a system that chooses an action in each state.
In this exhibit, you will compare three agents:
• a human agent (you)
• an untrained (random) agent (legal moves drawn uniformly at random)
• a Q-learning agent (learned Q-values → policy → actions)
All three are agents. The only difference is how they choose their actions in each state.
glossary.state:
STATE
A state is the current situation the agent "perceives". For a sliding puzzle, the state is the entire board configuration: which tile is in each position (including the empty space).
glossary.action:
ACTION
An action is a move the agent can choose. In a sliding puzzle, an action is a legal slide: move a neighbouring tile into the empty space (equivalently: move the empty space up, down, left, or right when allowed).
glossary.policy:
POLICY
A policy describes how an agent behaves. It is a rule that tells the agent which action to choose in each state.
In this exhibit, the Q-learning agent first learns Q-values. The policy is then derived from these values (for example, by picking the action with the highest Q-value).
Different agents follow different policies: a random agent follows a random policy, while a trained agent follows a learned policy.
glossary.rl:
REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
Reinforcement Learning is a framework for training an agent through interaction: the agent tries actions, receives feedback (rewards), and improves its behaviour over time. It is not a single algorithm but a family. More advanced examples: DQN on Atari (2015), AlphaZero for Go (2017).
In our puzzles, the reward is simple: +1 when the next state is the goal, 0 otherwise (an optional step penalty is available).
glossary.q:
Q-LEARNING
Q-learning is a reinforcement-learning algorithm. It learns values Q(state, action) that estimate how good each action is in each state. The agent then uses these Q-values to choose its actions (its policy).

params.episodesTip:
How many training episodes to run.
Each episode starts from a shuffled state.
params.maxStepsTip:
Safety cap: stop an episode if it has taken too many moves.
More steps lets the agent explore longer trajectories.
params.learningRateTip:
How much we overwrite old Q with new information.
α=1 means replace; smaller α means average slowly.
params.discountTip:
How much future rewards matter.
γ close to 1 values long-term success.
params.epsilonTip:
Exploration probability in ε-greedy.
With probability ε, pick a random action.
params.stepPenaltyTip:
Optional shaping: a small negative reward each move.
Encourages shorter solutions.
params.goalRewardTip:
Reward when the agent reaches the solved puzzle.
Default 1.
params.animSpeedTip:
How slowly to show moves while solving.
Increase for more time to watch.

stats.coverageTip: The Q-table is a dictionary — one entry per state visited. At 12 states it covers everything. At 181,440 it barely reaches a few percent: there are simply too many states to visit.
stats.costTip: On a laptop, one Q update costs about 10⁻¹¹ CHF (mostly hardware amortization, not electricity). A full Mission III comes to a fraction of a cent. Yet this tiny tariff becomes unreachable once the state space explodes: the same rule, at another scale, changes everything.
stats.budgetTip: Budget = episodes × max-steps-per-episode. The total number of Q-updates this training pass will perform. Larger budget can grow coverage — but on 181,440 states even a huge budget stays far from convergence guarantees.
stats.b5costTip:
Three levels of demand for solving B5 (the state farthest from the goal, 31 moves away):
• Demo (the agent often gets there): ~10⁷ steps ≈ 0.0001 CHF.
• Reliable (≥95% of runs succeed near the optimum): ~10⁹–10¹⁰ steps ≈ 0.01–0.1 CHF.
• Guaranteed (the agent plays near-perfectly everywhere): ~7×10¹³ steps ≈ 700 CHF.
Between 'reliable' and 'guaranteed', five orders of magnitude: that's where real RL practice lives.

params.episodesTip:
Episodes = number of training attempts.
Try 50–300 to see learning.
If ε is higher, you typically need more episodes.
params.maxStepsTip:
Max steps = move budget per episode.
Too small → never reach reward.
Try 15–40 for 2×2.
params.alphaTip:
α controls how strongly new evidence updates Q.
Q ← Q + α(target−Q).
0.05–0.2: stable but slow.
0.3–0.6: fast for this toy.
>0.8: noisy.
params.gammaTip:
γ controls how much future reward matters.
For delayed reward puzzles: γ≈0.9–0.99.
Low γ makes reward propagation weak.
params.epsilonTip:
ε = probability of a random legal move.
Try 0.05–0.25.
ε=0 early can lock in wrong beliefs.
params.speedTip:
Training runs in ticks.
0 = very fast.
Try 10–40 to watch Q propagate.

episode.def: A single attempt: shuffle the puzzle, try to solve it, stop on success or after max-steps moves, then start again with a fresh shuffle. More episodes = more independent experiences.

propagation.def: How the goal's reward travels back through Q-values, one episode at a time. The higher γ, the further the reward propagates backward through the state graph.

convergence.def: When Q-values stop changing meaningfully between episodes. The agent has "learned" the puzzle. On 360 states, this happens within a few thousand episodes; at larger scale, it is another story.

bench.titleTip:
Load a fixed start state, then run the current agent on it (greedy, no learning). Best score per benchmark is saved in this browser.
Theoretical minimum moves: B1: 1 | B2: 10 | B3: 18 | B4: 26 | B5: 31 (God's Number).

curse.def: When the state space grows, visiting every situation becomes impossible — there are simply too many cases. From M1 to M2 to M3, we go from 12 to 360 to 181,440 configurations. At the scale of chess (~10⁴⁴ positions), even a planet-sized computer wouldn't get through them. A Q-table becomes out of reach (Bellman, 1957).

generalisation.def: The ability of a learned function to give a reasonable value for states never seen during training. A Q-table has no generalisation — each state is a separate entry. A neural network (AlphaZero, Silver et al. 2018) learns a function that interpolates between nearby states.

budget.def: Total compute = episodes × max-steps-per-episode. Even at 10⁻¹¹ CHF per Q-update, the budget needed for guaranteed convergence on Mission III is many orders of magnitude beyond what a Saturday-afternoon laptop session produces.

m1.title: Make learning visible · 2×2
m1.napkinTitle: The Q-table fits on a napkin.
m1.napkinBody: 12 states × 2 actions per state = at most 24 rows. Build it by hand while the agent trains.
m1.benchHint: Each reference is a starting state at a fixed distance from the goal. The optimal distance is the length of the shortest solution.
m1.raceBody: Each team picks (α, γ, ε) three times with the same number of episodes. The table keeps score.

notes.1: 15 min · hook: have a human play against the random agent on the home-page mini-card. The You · Random comparison shows the why.
notes.2: 15 min · map the 12 configurations reachable from the goal. Build the Q-table by hand.
notes.3: Recommended parameters: α≈0.5 · γ≈0.9 · ε≈0.3 · 300 episodes. The max 2000 protects against runaway.
notes.4: If greedy fails: ε hit 0 too early, or the Q-table did not get enough episodes. Reset and rerun.

m2.title: Propagation · 2×3
m2.algoBody: With 360 states the table no longer fits on a page. Start training and watch Q propagate backward from the goal, episode after episode.
m2.raceBody: Each team picks (α, γ, ε) three times with the same number of episodes. The table keeps score.

notes.1: 10 min · open Mission II, watch the coverage gauge climb across 360 states in the first episodes.
notes.2: 15 min · train with the recommended parameters; benchmark each B1→B5; fill the race table.
notes.3: Recommended parameters: α≈0.3 · γ≈0.95 · ε≈0.4 · 2000 episodes. The max 20000 protects against runaway.
notes.4: Emphasise backward propagation: the reward travels back from the goal, one episode at a time (γ per hop).

m3.title: Scaling · 3×3
m3.curseBody: Over 181,440 states the coverage gauge plateaus far below 100%. On the Hub, the Training Economy card prices the curse in CHF: Demo 0.0001 · Reliable 0.01 · Guaranteed 700. Five orders of magnitude between hobby and guarantee.
m3.raceBody: Each team picks (α, γ, ε) three times with the same number of episodes. The table keeps score.

notes.1: 5 min · point at the Training Economy card: three pills Demo / Reliable / Guaranteed, five orders of magnitude between the first and the last.
notes.2: 20 min · train with the recommended parameters; aim for B5 (31 moves, antipode); watch the coverage gauge plateau.
notes.3: Recommended parameters: α≈0.3 · γ≈0.99 · ε≈0.5 · 10000 episodes. The max 50000 protects against runaway.
notes.4: Name the curse: same algorithm, same method, the space has simply grown too vast to visit. This is the doorway to neural networks — not a failure.

tune.title: Tuning the three knobs
tune.alpha: high: learns fast but may oscillate · low: stable but slow
tune.gamma: high: plans far ahead (more backward propagation) · low: myopic
tune.epsilon: high: explores more · too low too early: locks onto an initial choice
